papers.what_it_is: An experimental study that trains a data re-uploading quantum classifier on a single trapped barium ion, with no classical simulation guiding the training, and compares a genetic algorithm with BFGS gradient methods.

existing.note: The comparison is an ideal simulation with L-BFGS-B and a finite-difference step of 0.001 (Fig. 4(b)); no noiseless QPU was run. The 'if and only if' is the authors' inference from simulation, and the paper's noisy simulations (Fig. 5, Fig. A14) show BFGS-type solvers degrade with noise.
existing.value: The authors report that in an ideal simulation with the smallest step size 0.001, GA and BFGS are comparable in achievable accuracy and time to converge while gradient descent converges slowly, and they state that BFGS methods are only as good as GA if and only if the QPU is noiseless. The paper does not run a noiseless QPU.
quotes: Finally, as a comparison of ideal simulation with smallest step-size (0.001) we show in fig. (4(b)) that both GA and BFGS are comparable in terms of achievable accuracy and the time to converge but gradient descent shows slow convergence.
This indicates that BFGS methods are only as good as GA if and only if the QPU is noiseless.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result from one study; the iff statement is the authors' inference.
existing.reader_inference: The iff is not proved in the paper and no noiseless QPU run tests it.

existing.note: Two narrowings. (1) Only one of the two GA runs on the QPU exceeded 90 percent; the other stayed near 83 percent. (2) On the QPU only BFGS (finite difference at step 0.5, and analytic gradient) was run; SGD was not run on the QPU and the RL agent and gradient descent were run in simulation. The authors also state that step 0.5 is far too large for gradient-based algorithms to work well.

figures.shows: Structure of the four-year Bachelor of Quantum Engineering at UNSW as a grid of three terms per year. Year 1: Mathematics 1A, Electrical Circuits, Introduction to Engineering Design; Mathematics 1B, Physics 1A, Programming Fundamentals; Mathematics 2A, Physics 1B. Year 2: Circuits & Signals, Digital Circuit Design, Electromagnetic Engineering; Mathematics 2B, Analog Electronics, Engineering Design; Fundamentals of Quantum Engineering (marked A), Digital Signal Processing, General Education.
